toc.title: Identify Knowledge Critical to the Project (ECO)
Foster an Environment for Knowledge Transfer (ECO)
Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Term Meaning
Manage Project Knowledge Using existing knowledge and creating new knowledge to achieve project objectives and contribute to organizational learning
Explicit knowledge Formal and systematic; codifiable in words, pictures or numbers; easily communicated (manuals, procedures, documented processes); lacks context and can be misread
Tacit knowledge Embedded in a person's mind; personal, experience-based (skills, insights, practical judgment); hard to articulate and transfer; has context but is difficult to codify; shared through conversation and interaction
Knowledge management Tools and techniques that connect people to create new knowledge, share tacit knowledge and integrate the knowledge of diverse team members
Information management Tools and techniques that connect people to information, effective for simple, unambiguous, codified explicit knowledge (registers, libraries, search, PMIS)
Knowledge sharing and integration The key activities behind both reuse and creation: incorporating knowledge from different domains, context and project management
Lessons learned Knowledge gained during a project that shows how events were or should be addressed to improve future performance
Lessons learned register A project document or repository recording knowledge gained during a project, phase or iteration; created early in Manage Project Knowledge, then used as an input and updated in many processes; at the end it moves to the organization's lessons learned repository (an OPA)
Retrospective A regular workshop in which participants explore work and results to improve process and product; at least at the end of each iteration
After-action review (AAR) A structured review of what happened, why and how to do better, usually after a milestone or at the end
In-progress postmortem A structured review during the life cycle (not only at the end) to analyze current performance, issues and improvements
Critical knowledge Beyond PMBOK 8term Knowledge the project or its successors cannot do without, especially if held by one person or group at risk of leaving

2Explicit and Tacit Knowledge

  • Managing knowledge is more than documenting it or collecting lessons at project end. Codified knowledge lacks context; tacit knowledge has context but is hard to codify.
  • Objective: convert tacit knowledge into explicit knowledge when possible, while accepting that judgment is mostly shared through interaction.
  • Tacit knowledge is shared by fostering a collaborative, trust-filled environment: open communication, mentoring relationships, team building, face-to-face interactions and regular brainstorming. AI tools (for example interview bots) can help capture both kinds.
  • Tool choice depends on the project: the degree of innovation, complexity and the diversity (including of disciplines) among team members.

SECI knowledge conversion [Beyond PMBOK 8 — exam practice]: four ways knowledge changes form.

Mode From to Example
Socialization Tacit to tacit A new analyst sits with a veteran and picks up how she handles a difficult client
Externalization Tacit to explicit A retiring engineer talks through his troubleshooting rules and they are written up as a checklist
Combination Explicit to explicit Three departments' test reports are compiled into one summary
Internalization Explicit to tacit A new hire runs a documented deployment procedure again and again until it becomes second nature

3Manage Project Knowledge: the Process

Aspect Detail
Benefits Use prior organizational knowledge to produce or improve the outcome; collect new knowledge to support operations and future projects or phases
Inputs Project management plan, lessons learned register, team assignments, resource breakdown structure, stakeholder register, deliverables, EEFs, OPAs
Tools Expert judgment, knowledge management, information management, after-action reviews, in-progress postmortems, storytelling, retrospective meetings, interpersonal skills (active listening, facilitation, leadership, networking, political awareness)
Outputs Lessons learned register, project management plan updates, OPA updates
Plan it Decide how and when lessons learned and retrospectives will happen throughout the project; identify what information to collect during the project and at closure; set how historical information and lessons will be made available to current and future projects
Who The people and teams involved in the work capture the lessons; knowledge can be recorded in video, pictures, audio or other suitable media
AI Can be a significant source of knowledge, but risks include exposing sensitive information and hallucinations; projects should have responsible AI policies (Topic 08)

4Identify Knowledge Critical to the Project (ECO)

Questions to ask [Beyond PMBOK 8 structure]:

  1. What must the project, the next phase, operations or maintenance be able to do that depends on specific know-how?
  2. Who holds it? Look for single points of failure: experts, senior engineers, vendor specialists, SMEs, retirees, people whose assignment is ending.
  3. What is the risk of losing it, and what would the loss cost (schedule, safety, compliance, quality)?
  4. How hard is it to replace or rebuild? (judgment and troubleshooting skills are far harder than procedures)
  5. What knowledge from earlier projects do we need now? (lessons learned, historical information, similar projects' delays and fixes)

Tools: skill matrix, stakeholder and resource registers, risk register (record knowledge loss as a risk with an owner and a response), interviews, transition and succession plans.

Timing: early in planning, whenever staffing changes, and before a person, crew or contractor is released (the window closes when they leave). Identify and capture knowledge from people first; documents can be reviewed afterward.

5Gather Knowledge (ECO)

Explicit knowledge:

  • Record lessons in the lessons learned register (category and description of the situation; impacts; recommendations; proposed actions) including challenges, problems, realized risks and opportunities. Capture continuously, not only at closure; at the end transfer to the lessons learned repository.
  • Make records searchable and categorized so people can find them; add a way to contact the originator ("contact me" function) because asking is faster than guessing keywords.
  • Use information management tools: library services, web searches, PMIS and document management systems.

Tacit knowledge:

  • After-action reviews: four questions: what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why were there differences, what can we learn?
  • Retrospectives at least every iteration; in-progress postmortems at stages of the life cycle.
  • Work shadowing and reverse shadowing, pairing, mentoring, storytelling, interviews (including AI interview bots), learning-review workshops, brainstorming.
  • Storytelling conveys lessons, good practice and outcomes in a relatable, memorable way; it is particularly effective for tacit knowledge and can shape culture.

6Foster an Environment for Knowledge Transfer (ECO)

Condition How to build it
Trust and psychological safety People share mistakes and insights when they will not be punished; leaders model openness; blameless reviews
Open communication and collaboration Regular conversations, brainstorming, face-to-face and virtual collaboration tools; communities of practice, special interest groups, discussion forums
Time and space Schedule retrospectives, reviews, knowledge cafés and fairs, seminars and interactive training; protect that time
Mentoring and shadowing Mix experience levels; pair successors with experts during the work
Hands-on transfer Receivers practice the task with support before handover (watching is not doing); pair local staff with a vendor specialist during installation and commissioning
Accessible, usable repository Searchable lessons, clear categories, owners; walk the next team through the key lessons instead of just sending a log
Connection to process owners Link knowledge tools to project processes and process owners; communities and subject matter experts can generate insights that improve control processes; an internal sponsor helps implement improvements
Incentives and recognition Recognize sharing and use of lessons
Responsible AI use Approved tools, protection of sensitive data, human review of outputs

7Applying Knowledge

  • Pull earlier lessons into the plan. Where a previous project's delays had specific causes (late permits, commissioning problems), adjust the plan to address those causes, not with a generic buffer.
  • Analyze lessons for patterns: recurring issues point to changes in project procedures and checklists (Topic 31).
  • Feed OPAs: lessons learned repository, templates, standards, checklists (consolidate best practices into one standard rather than leaving teams with their own).
  • Hand over to operations or the next phase: transition with practice and support; confirm the receivers can operate or continue the work (Topic 35).
  • Check use: if the next team says logs were never useful, the problem is accessibility and interaction, not more detail in the log.

8Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Cadence Lessons at phase ends and gates, plus in-progress postmortems; final lessons at closure Retrospective every iteration; review and demo events; continuous sharing Retrospectives inside iterations, gate reviews for the envelope
Tacit transfer Mentoring, shadowing, handover training Pairing, swarming, cross-functional teams, shared ownership Both
Records Lessons learned register, formal repository Lightweight shared notes, backlog improvements, working agreements Both
Actions Update plans, procedures, OPAs A few improvements committed into the next iteration's backlog Both
Beyond PMBOK 8 Pair programming, mob sessions, communities of practice across teams

9Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

  • Tailor to project type (innovative or complex projects need more interaction), team diversity and distribution (virtual teams need deliberate tools and relationship time), organizational culture, regulation and records requirements, security needs, and the use of AI.
  • Interactions: knowledge links to resources (team continuity, skills), communication (storytelling, transparency), risk (knowledge loss risks), quality and improvement (lessons drive process change), procurement (vendor knowledge and handover), and closure (final lessons and transition).
  • Signs of effective knowledge management: critical knowledge is known and not held by one person; lessons are captured as work proceeds and are actually used; people can find what they need; receivers can perform handed-over work; sharing is normal and safe.

10Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Tacit knowledge needs interaction: shadowing, pairing, mentoring, hands-on practice. Documents alone will not carry judgment.
  2. Capture critical knowledge from people before they leave; do not wait for closure, and do not start with document reviews.
  3. Watching is not doing: receivers should perform the task with support before handover.
  4. Capture lessons continuously (retrospectives, AARs, in-progress postmortems), not only at the end.
  5. Lessons must be usable: searchable, categorized, owned, and walked through with the next team; more detail in an unused log changes nothing.
  6. Use earlier lessons in the plan, specifically, instead of adding a generic buffer.
  7. Make knowledge loss a risk: register it, assign an owner and plan the transfer.
  8. Psychological safety matters: if people stay silent in retrospectives, fix the environment and follow through on actions.
  9. Use AI responsibly: approved tools, no sensitive data exposure, verify outputs.
  10. Convert tacit to explicit when possible, but do not assume it all can be.
  11. Connect people: communities of practice, forums and networks reduce duplicated problem-solving across teams.
  12. A lessons learned register is created early and updated throughout, then moved to the organization's repository.
  13. Commit to a few improvements from retrospectives and put them in the backlog; a long list with no owner is not learning.
  14. Include vendors and contractors: transfer vendor expertise to the people who will maintain the system.

11Exam Q&A

11.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A retiring planner can sense which suppliers will deliver late from small signs in their behavior, although the company holds detailed supplier scorecards. What kind of knowledge is at risk, and how is it best transferred?

  • ATacit knowledge, best transferred by asking the planner to write a final report
  • BExplicit knowledge, best transferred by adding more fields to the scorecards
  • CTacit knowledge, best transferred by working alongside the planner and discussing cases
  • DExplicit knowledge, best transferred by copying the scorecards to the successor
Show the answer

Answer: C. Judgment drawn from experience is tacit knowledge, which passes through interaction such as shadowing, pairing and discussion of real cases. Scorecards hold explicit data, and a written report after departure lacks the context and the chance to ask questions.

S2Staff need to find approved standards and templates quickly, and the knowledge is codified and unambiguous. Which kind of tool fits best?

  • AStorytelling sessions in which senior staff recount their earlier projects
  • BInformation management tools, such as a searchable library or PMIS
  • CAn after-action review held after each template has been used
  • DKnowledge management through a community of practice that meets once a quarter
Show the answer

Answer: B. Information management connects people to information and works well for simple, codified, explicit knowledge such as standards and templates. Communities, stories and reviews are knowledge management techniques suited to tacit or context-rich knowledge.

S3After a release milestone, the project manager wants a structured conversation about what happened and why. Which set of questions does an after-action review use?

  • AWhat was supposed to happen, what happened, why they differ, and what can be learned
  • BWho caused the delay, who will pay for it, and who will be reassigned afterward
  • CWhat the plan said, what the contract said, and what the sponsor now wants
  • DWhat went well, what went badly, and what grade each person should receive
Show the answer

Answer: A. An after-action review asks four questions: what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why there were differences and what can be learned. Blaming, comparing documents or grading individuals does not produce learning.

S4The hybrid project depends on one engineer who alone understands a legacy interface and has just handed in a resignation notice. What is the best way to treat this in the plan?

  • AAccept the situation and rely on the manual that the engineer wrote years ago
  • BRecord knowledge loss as a risk with an owner and plan the transfer before departure
  • CAsk the engineer to write documentation after leaving, under a consulting contract
  • DRedesign the legacy interface from scratch without involving the engineer
Show the answer

Answer: B. Knowledge held by one person is a single point of failure, so its loss is registered as a risk with an owner and a plan to transfer it while the person is present. Writing afterward, a redesign without the expert or relying on an old manual leaves the risk in place.

S5Lessons in the organization's repository are well categorized, but readers say they cannot ask the people behind them what the entries mean. What small addition would help most?

  • AA requirement that all lessons are reviewed and approved by the PMO
  • BA way to contact the originator of each lesson, since asking is faster than guessing
  • CA longer description of each lesson, written in more formal language
  • DA monthly report listing the lessons that were added to the repository
Show the answer

Answer: B. Searchable, categorized lessons work best with a way to contact the originator, because asking is faster and gives context that a record lacks. Longer entries, activity reports or an approval gate do not provide that interaction.

S6After the project manager publicly criticized a member for admitting a mistake in a retrospective, nobody has shared a problem. How should the project manager restore sharing?

  • AWait for the team to forget and then restart the sessions as before
  • BMake attendance at lessons sessions mandatory and record who spoke
  • CSwitch to anonymous written lessons only and stop holding sessions
  • DAcknowledge the error, model openness and run blameless reviews
Show the answer

Answer: D. Sharing needs trust and psychological safety, which a leader rebuilds by owning the mistake, modeling openness, using blameless reviews and following through on agreed actions. Forced attendance, abandoning sessions or waiting leaves the damage in place.

S7A successor has shadowed an expert for a month, and the expert leaves in two weeks. Which technique best confirms that the successor can do the job?

  • AAnother month of shadowing, with the successor taking notes during each task
  • BA recorded video of the expert performing the work, for later viewing
  • CA written test of the procedures that the successor has read
  • DReverse shadowing, with the expert watching the successor perform the work
Show the answer

Answer: D. Watching is not doing: reverse shadowing has the expert observe the successor performing the work, which confirms competence while the expert can still correct and advise. More note-taking, a written test or a recording does not test performance.

S8A senior estimator's rules of thumb are only partly written down. Which approach to capturing them is best?

  • ASkip documentation altogether, since the knowledge is tacit and cannot be recorded
  • BAssume all of it can be turned into a manual and stop the conversations
  • CCodify what can be written, and keep mentoring for the judgment
  • DRecord the estimator's final estimates only, without any of the reasoning
Show the answer

Answer: C. The aim is to convert tacit knowledge to explicit form where possible while accepting that judgment is mostly shared through interaction, so both documentation and mentoring are used. Assuming everything can be codified, recording nothing or recording only results loses either context or judgment.

S9To recover a delay, the sponsor suggests canceling the team's retrospectives and lessons sessions for the next quarter. What should the project manager do?

  • AAgree and ask the team to record lessons in writing after the quarter ends
  • BKeep only the end-of-project lessons session and cancel all the others
  • CExplain that the sessions drive improvement and protect the time for them
  • DHold the sessions after hours so that they do not reduce working time
Show the answer

Answer: C. Knowledge sharing needs time and space that is protected in the schedule, and retrospectives pay back through improvement. Postponing to the end of the quarter, keeping only a final session or pushing the sessions after hours discards or penalizes the learning.

S10Nobody uses the lessons learned repository, and no one is recognized for adding to it or using it. What should the project manager do?

  • APenalize teams that repeat a mistake already recorded as a lesson
  • BTell all team members that they must use the repository and monitor their logins
  • CMove the repository to a new tool and announce the change by email
  • DRecognize sharing and use of lessons, and link them to project processes
Show the answer

Answer: D. Incentives and recognition for sharing and using lessons, together with links to project processes and their owners, create an environment where knowledge is actually reused. Mandates, a new tool or penalties do not change behavior.

S11The project management plan says nothing about how lessons will be captured, who will review them or how they will reach future projects. What should the project manager do?

  • AAdd a plan for when lessons are captured and how they are shared
  • BLeave the matter until closing, when all lessons can be collected at once
  • CAsk the PMO to collect the lessons directly from the sponsor later
  • DCreate the lessons learned register at closure and fill it from memory
Show the answer

Answer: A. Manage Project Knowledge is planned: how and when lessons and retrospectives happen, what information is collected, and how historical information reaches current and future projects, with the register created early. Waiting for closure or relying on memory loses the knowledge.

S12An R&D project brings together experts from five disciplines, but findings stay within each discipline because everyone relies on a shared document library. What should the project manager add?

  • ARegular cross-discipline interaction, such as brainstorming sessions
  • BA rule that experts may only share findings that are fully validated
  • CA larger document library with stricter indexing of every report
  • DA quarterly report summarizing each discipline's findings for the others
Show the answer

Answer: A. Knowledge management connects people to create and share new knowledge, so complex, innovative work with diverse disciplines needs more interaction than document storage. A bigger library, quarterly summaries or validation-only rules keep knowledge in silos.

11.2 Recall Q&As

R1Explicit versus tacit knowledge?

Show the answer

Explicit is codifiable, formal and easily shared; tacit is personal, experience-based, hard to articulate and shared through interaction.

R2Knowledge management versus information management?

Show the answer

Knowledge management connects people to create and share (mostly tacit) knowledge; information management connects people to codified information.

R3Name knowledge management techniques.

Show the answer

Networking, communities of practice, work shadowing and reverse shadowing, discussion forums, seminars, workshops and learning reviews, creativity techniques, knowledge fairs and cafés, interactive training.

R4What are the four AAR questions?

Show the answer

What was supposed to happen? What actually happened? Why were there differences? What can we learn?

R5How does an in-progress postmortem differ from a traditional one?

Show the answer

It is held periodically during the life cycle to improve continuously, not only at the end.

R6What is a retrospective and how often is it held?

Show the answer

A regular workshop to improve process and product, at least at the end of each iteration; it produces actionable improvements with owners.

R7What does the lessons learned register contain, and when is it created?

Show the answer

Category and description of the situation, impacts, recommendations and proposed actions (including problems and realized risks and opportunities); created early as an output of Manage Project Knowledge and updated throughout.

R8Where do lessons go at the end of the project?

Show the answer

To the organization's lessons learned repository, an organizational process asset.

R9Work shadowing versus reverse shadowing?** **[Beyond PMBOK 8 definitions; PMBOK 8 only lists both terms]

Show the answer

In shadowing the learner follows the expert; in reverse shadowing the expert observes the learner doing the work.

R10Why is storytelling effective?

Show the answer

It makes lessons relatable and memorable, transfers tacit knowledge and shapes culture.

R11What are the risks of AI in knowledge management?

Show the answer

Unintentional exposure of sensitive information and AI hallucinations; use responsible AI policies.

R12What is the objective regarding tacit knowledge?

Show the answer

Convert it into explicit knowledge when possible.

R13Who captures lessons learned?

Show the answer

The people and teams involved in the work.

R14What affects the choice of knowledge management tools?

Show the answer

The degree of innovation, project complexity and the diversity of team members, including diversity of disciplines.

12Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Process Manage Project Knowledge: use existing knowledge, create new knowledge, support organizational learning
Explicit Codifiable, formal, easily shared; lacks context
Tacit Personal, experience-based, hard to articulate; shared through interaction
Tools Information management (registers, libraries, PMIS) vs knowledge management (networking, communities, shadowing, workshops)
Lessons learned register Created early; updated throughout; to the organization's repository at close
Retrospective At least each iteration; actionable items
AAR What was supposed to happen, what happened, why different, what to learn
In-progress postmortem Periodic review during the life cycle
Identify critical knowledge Who holds it, what if they leave, how hard to replace; before people are released
Gather Documents plus shadowing, pairing, interviews, storytelling; continuously
Foster Trust, safety, time, mentoring, hands-on practice, accessible repository, process owners
Handover Receivers perform with support before handover
Use lessons Apply specifically in planning; update OPAs and checklists
AI Responsible policies; protect sensitive data; verify outputs
First-action pattern Identify critical knowledge and who holds it, capture from people now, transfer through practice, make lessons usable, apply and update OPAs
